_meta.scope: CMS-A Introductory Sommelier: syllabus scope (Part A), France chapter (Part B), France flashcards (Part C).
notes: Every fact was taken from a page or PDF fetched on 2026-10-31; the source URL is on each fact. CMS PDF links carry #page=N for the page the fact is on.

No Wine Folly or GuildSomm pages were needed; all region facts come from official bodies or the CMS guide.
French-language INAO and InterLoire text was translated; those facts are marked '(Translated from French)'.

CMS Curriculum Guide is dated 8.2023; some region rules have changed since (e.g. Champagne added Chardonnay Rose in 2025; Saint-Émilion 2022 list). Where the region body and CMS differ, both are given.

documents.fact: CMS-A Resource Library lists, for the Introductory Sommelier level: Course Guide (What To Expect), Course Syllabus, Course Practice Exam, Course Tasting Journal, Grape Variety Profiles, Course & Certified Sommelier Theory Exam Curriculum Guide, Online Examination Guide, Online Course Wines List.
Introductory Sommelier Course and Exam Syllabus (footer dated 1.2024): covers course details, policies and expectations. For exam content it points to the Course Guide and the Curriculum Guide.
Course Guide: What to Expect and How to Prepare (footer dated 1.2024): holds the course outline (Sections 1-12), learning objectives and the exam content list.

Introductory Sommelier Course and Certified Sommelier Theory Exam Curriculum Guide (footer dated 8.2023): subject-by-subject topic framework with an 'Introductory Level' column and a 'Certified Sommelier Exam' column. It says a blank topic for a subject means that information is not essential at that level.

The syllabus says the Introductory Sommelier Course Workbook and the Curriculum Guide narrow the scope of the course and should be the primary resource for the exam. A PDF of the workbook comes with registration; a print copy is optional (Amazon). A one-month GuildSomm trial is included.

exam_format.fact: Closed-book exam: 70 multiple-choice questions, four answer options each, 45 minutes, Scantron answer sheet.
Pass mark is 60%, i.e. 42 of 70 correct; each correct answer is worth one point.
Questions are based on the published learning objectives, the Introductory Sommelier Course Guide and study resources such as the Introductory Sommelier Course Workbook.
Students who score under 60% may retake online for $150, waiting at least 14 days after the last attempt.
Prerequisites: no previous experience or courses; students must be 21 or older. Course is two days (in person 8:00 AM-6:00 PM); exam at 4:00 PM on Day 2.
The syllabus names the course audience as servers, bartenders, support staff, and entry-level retail or distribution staff in beverage and hospitality.

four_pillars.fact: CMS-A's four pillars of education and examination: Theory; Tasting; Hospitality and Service; Business of the Sommelier.

learning_objectives.fact: Have a general appreciation of the breadth of global beverage alcohol offerings.
Identify historically and commercially important wine regions of the world and know their respective grape varieties and styles.
Evaluate and describe 20 classic wines of the world.
Understand the Deductive Tasting Method to build vocabulary and skills for objective evaluation and description of classic wines and major grape varieties.
Recognize and explain climatic and winemaking effects on wine style.
Receive an introduction to service and hospitality by observing the formal mechanical service of still and sparkling wine by the bottle.
Learn the basic principles of food and beverage pairing and how to apply these principles to different styles of food and wine.
Learn the fundamentals of beer, sake, spirits, and liqueurs.

exam_content_areas.fact: Wine law of important regions: connecting grape varieties with specific places or appellations, and appellations with the style(s) of wine produced.
Wine production methods: still, sparkling, fortified, sweet.

Important historical figures in wine mentioned in the book and/or lectures; examples given: Agoston Haraszthy, Robert Mondavi, André Tchelistcheff, David Lett, Dr. Konstantine Frank (spelling as printed in the guide).
Wine and food pairing: principles, interactions and classic pairings.
Map identification: recognition of important world wine regions.
Reading a wine label: determining grape variety, colour and style from the label.
Beverage service basics. The guide says there is no need to memorise service temperatures at this level.
How wines and grape varieties look, smell and taste, focusing on wines tasted in class.
Producer recognition in major regions. Examples given for Bordeaux: the First Growths of the 1855 Classification of the Médoc; Saint-Émilion: Château Cheval Blanc; Pomerol: Château Pétrus.
Soil types, for major regions only. Examples given: Champagne, Chablis, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Bordeaux Right and Left Bank, Mosel, Coonawarra.
Beer basics (main ingredients, common styles); sake basics (ingredients, quality scale); spirits basics (base ingredients, common styles).

not_tested.fact: Not tested at the Introductory exam: wine tasting, performance of service elements, vintage memorisation.

curriculum_guide_subjects_in_order.fact: Curriculum Guide subject order: Grape Growing - Viticulture (p3); Winemaking - Vinification (p7); France - Bordeaux (p9); France - Burgundy (p12); France - Loire Valley (p15); France - The Rhône Valley (p17); France - Champagne (p19); France - Alsace (p21); France - South France, Certified exam only (p23); Italy - Piedmont (p26); Italy - Lombardy & Emilia-Romagna (p28); Italy - Trentino-Alto Adige / Friuli / Veneto (p30); Italy - Tuscany (p32); Italy - Central & Southern Italy (p34); Italy - Sicily & Sardinia (p36); Spain - Galicia (p37); Spain - La Rioja (p38); Spain - Castilla y León (p40); Spain - Catalonia (p42); Spain - Other DOs, Certified only (p44); Portugal (p46); Germany (p47); Austria (p52); Hungary (p54); Greece, Certified only (p55); California North Coast (p56); California Central Coast (p58); New York State (p60); Pacific Northwest (p61); Canada (p63); México (p65); Chile (p67); Argentina (p69); South Africa (p71); New Zealand (p73); Australia (p75); World Sparkling Wines (p77); Sweet Wines (p79); Fortified Wines (p81); Beer (p83); Sake (p86); Spirits & Liqueurs (p88); Cocktails (p92); Business of the Sommelier (p93).

Each region page uses the same row headings: Geography (Location, Climate Category, Physical Features), Wine: White Grape Variety Names, Wine: Red Grape Variety Names, Soil, Grape Growing, Winemaking, Style, Wine Law / Appellations / Classification, Label Terms, General Terms, Producers / Proprietary Brand, Vintage, History & Lore, Service of Beverage, Food and Beverage Pairing, Business of the Sommelier (BOS). A manual chapter per region can follow this order.
Note: the Course Guide orders France as Champagne, Burgundy, Bordeaux, Loire, Alsace, Rhône; the Curriculum Guide orders it Bordeaux, Burgundy, Loire, Rhône, Champagne, Alsace.

bordeaux.fact: Learning outcome (Intro): locate and recognise major Bordeaux appellations; know the important grapes, bodies of water and soil types; basics of the Bordeaux classification systems; recognise names and labels of important châteaux; begin to connect weather, vintage, style and price.
Location: Southwest France, along the Atlantic coast. Climate: maritime to continental moving from the coast inland. Bodies of water: Atlantic Ocean, Gironde Estuary, Garonne River, Dordogne River.
Grapes (Intro): white - Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, small amounts of Muscadelle; red - Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, small amounts of Malbec, Petit Verdot, Carménère.
Soils: gravel, clay, limestone, sand; grapes are matched to soil, e.g. Cabernet Sauvignon in gravel and Merlot in clay.
Grape growing: humidity from large bodies of water and spring rain contributes to mould and rot; humidity helps noble rot for sweet wine, especially in Sauternes.
Winemaking: blends; dry whites; dry reds; botrytis-affected sweet wines; use of new French oak for red and white.

Appellations (Intro): Regional - Bordeaux AOC. Left Bank - Médoc AOP, Haut-Médoc AOP; communes Margaux, Pauillac, St-Estèphe, St-Julien; Graves AOP with Pessac-Léognan and Sauternes; Entre-Deux-Mers AOP; Right Bank - Pomerol AOP, St-Émilion AOP, St-Émilion Grand Cru AOP. Identify each on a map and the wine types made.

Classification (Intro): 1855 Classification history; First Growths: Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Mouton Rothschild, Margaux, Haut-Brion. Pomerol: no classification. St-Émilion: multi-tiered classification, revised periodically, highly controversial.

Producers to recognise (Intro): Lafite Rothschild (Pauillac), Latour (Pauillac), Mouton Rothschild (Pauillac), Margaux (Margaux), Haut-Brion (Graves), d'Yquem (Sauternes), Petrus (Pomerol), Ausone (St-Émilion), Cheval-Blanc (St-Émilion).

History & lore (Intro): marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine; Dutch innovation and exportation; slave trade port; today the largest region of AOP wine production in France; global image and evolution of market and style.
Food pairing (Intro): bold reds with beef and lamb; rich sweet wines with dessert and foie gras.

burgundy.fact: Learning outcome (Intro): identify Burgundy and its five major regions on a map; history, prominent soils, the classification hierarchy and grapes for each area; recognise major villages and significant vineyards in the Côte d'Or.
Location: set of five non-contiguous regions in eastern France. Climate: cool continental. Physical features: hills, aspect and slope.
Grapes (Intro): white - Chardonnay, Aligoté (small amounts); red - Pinot Noir, Gamay.
Soils (Intro): Chablis and Côte d'Or - limestone, clay; Beaujolais - granite.
Winemaking (Intro): malolactic fermentation; carbonic maceration; use of new French oak. Styles: dry whites, dry reds.
Regions on a map (Intro): 1. Chablis; 2. Côte d'Or (Côte de Nuits, Côte de Beaune); 3. Côte Chalonnaise; 4. Mâconnais; 5. Beaujolais.
Hierarchy (Intro): Regional AOP / Villages AOP / Premier Cru AOP / Grand Cru AOP. Regional AOP: Bourgogne AOP. Chablis AOP: Village / Premier Cru / Grand Cru; recognise Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos.

Côte de Nuits villages (Intro): Gevrey-Chambertin, Morey-St.-Denis, Chambolle-Musigny, Vougeot, Vosne-Romanée, Nuits-St.-Georges. Côte de Beaune villages: Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Chassagne-Montrachet, Puligny-Montrachet.
Beaujolais (Intro): Beaujolais-Villages / Beaujolais Cru; recognise the Beaujolais Cru Morgon.
Label terms (Intro): Négociant, Domaine, Clos, Monopole, Vieilles Vignes.
History & lore (Intro): Monastic and Napoleonic Code of Inheritance influences on classification, fragmentation of vineyards and ownership.

loire.fact: Location: from the Atlantic coast to central France. Four regions west to east: Pays Nantais, Anjou-Saumur, Touraine, Central Vineyards.
Physical feature: the Loire is the longest river in France, beginning in the Massif Central.
Climates (Intro): Pays Nantais cool and wet maritime; Anjou-Saumur maritime moving toward continental, humid; Touraine continental; Central Vineyards continental.

Appellations (Intro): Pays Nantais - Muscadet, Muscadet de Sèvre-et-Maine; Anjou-Saumur - Saumur, Saumur-Champigny, Savennières, Quarts-de-Chaume, Bonnezeaux; Touraine - Chinon, Bourgueil, Vouvray; Central Vineyards - Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé.
Soil (Intro): tuffeau in Vouvray. Botrytis in Bonnezeaux and Quarts-de-Chaume due to humidity from multiple rivers.
Winemaking (Intro): Muscadet - sur lie aging; Saumur - traditional method sparkling, dry whites, dry reds, lusciously sweet wines; Vouvray can be sparkling, dry, off-dry and sweet.
Grapes (Intro): Muscadet - Melon B (formerly Melon de Bourgogne); Anjou-Saumur and Touraine - Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc; Central Vineyards - Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir.
Label terms (Intro): Sur lie, Sec, Demi-Sec. (Moelleux is listed in the Certified column.)

rhone.fact: Location (Intro): between Burgundy and Provence; a 30-mile gap between the Northern and Southern Rhône. The Rhône river starts in Switzerland and flows south through France to the Mediterranean.
Climate: Northern Rhône moderate continental; Southern Rhône Mediterranean.
Physical features (Intro): Northern Rhône steep hillsides; Southern Rhône flatter terrain.
Soils: Northern Rhône decomposed granite, schist; Southern Rhône galets, alluvial, limestone.
Grape growing (Intro): North - terraced slopes with staked vines against the Mistral; South - traditionally bush vines to conserve water and give shade.
Winemaking (Intro): co-fermented wines in the north; blended wines in the south.
Grapes (Intro): North white - Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne; North red - Syrah. South white - Grenache Blanc; South red - Grenache, Mourvèdre.
Northern Rhône AOPs (Intro): Côte Rôtie, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, St.-Joseph, Condrieu, Cornas; note the styles made in each.

Southern Rhône tiers (Intro): Côtes-du-Rhône AOP; Côtes-du-Rhône Villages AOP (named villages); Crus/single village examples: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Tavel, Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise.

Label terms (Intro): Vins Doux Naturels, example Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise. General terms: Cru (single village); co-fermentation (which northern AOP uses it). Style: spicy, meaty reds; rich, aromatic whites. History: Papal occupation.

champagne.fact: Learning outcome (Intro): identify Champagne on a map, know its grape varieties, and define what makes Champagne unique by understanding the Champagne Method.

Location: 49th parallel, one of the most northerly wine regions. Climate: cool continental. No protection from Atlantic influence, so unpredictable weather, rain, frost and hail threats. Soil: limestone, chalk.
Grape growing: grapes are picked earlier to preserve natural acidity.

Champagne Method steps (Intro): still wine is made; assemblage of cuvée; bubbles created using liqueur de tirage; sur lie aging - autolysis; riddling (remuage) using pupitre or gyropalette; disgorging (dégorgement); dosage added using liqueur d'expédition.
Grapes (Intro): white - Chardonnay; red - Pinot Noir, Meunier.
Appellation (Intro): Champagne AOP; subregions Vallée de la Marne, Côte des Blancs, Montagne de Reims.
Aging (Intro): Non-Vintage 12 months on lees, minimum 15 months total aging; Vintage minimum 36 months total aging.

Label terms (Intro): Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs, Brut. General terms: Cuvée de Prestige/Tête de Cuvée, Négociant, Grower. Styles: Brut, Non-Vintage, Vintage, Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs, Rosé.
Producers (Intro): Moët & Chandon, Roederer, Veuve Clicquot, Taittinger, Charles Heidsieck, Krug.

Service (Intro): never point the cork at someone while opening, and never take your hand off the top (cage and cork) while removing the cork. History: invention of the riddling rack (Madame Clicquot) and gyropalette.

alsace.fact: Learning outcome (Intro): recognise and locate Alsace, identify its main grapes, and understand how geography and history affect its styles.
Location: northeastern France, on the border with Germany. Climate: cool, continental with a dry, sunny growing season. Physical features: Vosges Mountains, Rhine River.
Grape growing (Intro): the Vosges create a rain shadow; one of France's driest and sunniest climates; better vineyards on slopes facing east/southeast; over 90% of Alsace wines are from white grapes.
Winemaking (Intro): large neutral casks, little to no new oak; sparkling, dry, off-dry and sweet wines are made.
Grapes (Intro): white - Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat; red - Pinot Noir.

Wine law (Intro): must be 100% of the grape variety if the name is on the label. Alsace/Vin d'Alsace AOP is the main appellation. Alsace Grand Cru AOP: 51 Grand Cru vineyards. Crémant d'Alsace AOP: traditional method sparkling.
Grand Cru grapes (Intro): traditionally only Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer, Muscat; the curriculum adds 'the fifth is now Pinot Noir as of the 2022 vintage'.
Styles (Intro): Vendange Tardive (VT) - late-harvest, rich, full-bodied, not always sweet. Sélection de Grains Nobles (SGN) - botrytis-affected grapes, small quantities, only in top vintages.
History (Intro): history of French and German rule; distinctive culture in architecture, language and food.

south_france.fact: South France (Provence, Languedoc-Roussillon, Southwest, Dordogne) is marked 'Certified Sommelier Exam only', so it is outside the Introductory scope.

facts.fact: CMS-A publishes a public Introductory Sommelier Course Practice Examination PDF in its Resource Library.
The practice exam PDF has 70 numbered questions and an answer key. Questions are not copied here.
The Course Guide points to practice-exam questions 3 and 62 (label reading), 15 (service) and 58 and 64 (how wines look, smell, taste) as examples of exam content types.

other_cms_resources.fact: Grape Variety Profiles (Introductory Level) PDF is also in the Resource Library.

aoc_system.fact: AOP (appellation d'origine protégée) designates a product whose production steps are all carried out according to recognised know-how in one geographical area, which gives the product its characteristics. It is a European sign protecting the name throughout the EU. (Translated from French.)

AOC (appellation d'origine contrôlée) is a compulsory national recognition step before a name is registered as an AOP at European level. Only wine products keep the right to carry the term 'AOC' if they wish. (Translated from French.)
AOP rules are written in a specification (cahier des charges) set by producers and approved by the EU, and are checked by an independent body approved by INAO. (Translated from French.)
The Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée was established in 1935; the European-level AOP was created in 1992 and gives the same guarantees.
An Appellation of Origin is a delimited area plus a specification of production rules; it is recognised in French law as 'Contrôlée' and at EU level as 'Protégée' (English: PDO).

The Rhône's Baron Le Roy (Châteauneuf-du-Pape) championed the AOC system in the 1930s; his specification (delimited area, grape varieties, local practices, cultivation methods, minimum alcohol, harvest period) became the model for later AOC decrees. He presided over INAO from 1947 to 1967.

label_tiers.fact: French wines fall into two main categories: wines with a geographical indication (AOC/AOP or PDO, and IGP or PGI) and wines without one (VSIG, sometimes labelled Vin de France, or Vin Mousseux for sparkling).
IGP (Protected Geographical Indication) replaced the old Vin de Pays (VdP) and is the intermediate category of wines.

INAO: an IGP identifies a product whose quality, reputation or other characteristics are linked to its geographical origin; at least one stage of production, processing or preparation must take place in the delimited area. (Translated from French.)
VSIG (wine without geographical indication) replaced the old Vins de Table. It may show grape variety and/or vintage on the label and can carry 'Vin de France' or 'Vin de Cépage de France'.

manual_tiers_summary.fact: Top to bottom for a staff manual: AOC/AOP (most rules, smallest named areas) > IGP (formerly Vin de Pays) > Vin de France / VSIG (formerly Vin de Table).
manual_tiers_summary.note: Ordering combines the Inter Rhône pyramid, IGP and VSIG glossary entries.

location_climate.fact: Champagne lies about 150 km north-east of Paris; the Champagne AOC production area was defined by a law of 1927, covers around 34,200 hectares and is the most northerly of France's vineyards.
Dual climate with both oceanic and continental influences; average annual temperature 11°C. Reims is at 49°5' N and Épernay at 49° N, near the limit for quality grapes.
Subsoil outcrops are 75% limestone (chalk, marl and limestone proper). Chalk is porous and stores 300-400 litres of water per m3.
CMS: 49th parallel, cool continental; no protection from Atlantic influence, so unpredictable weather, rain, frost and hail. Soil: limestone, chalk.

grapes.fact: Three main grapes: Pinot Noir (black), Meunier (black), Chardonnay (white).
2025 vine population: Pinot Noir 38%, Chardonnay 32%, Meunier 30%.
grapes.note: The grape-varieties page gives 38% / 31% / 31% and the CMS guide gives 38% Pinot Noir, 30% Chardonnay, 32% Meunier. Shares shift year to year.

grapes.fact: Other authorised white grapes: Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris and, since 2025, Chardonnay Rose. Together they are about 0.3% of plantings.
grapes.note: The FAQ lists only four (no Chardonnay Rose) at under 0.4%; the grape page is the newer statement.

grapes.fact: Pinot Noir dominates Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar (83% of Côte des Bar vines); Chardonnay is the star of Côte des Blancs; Meunier, which buds later and resists frost better, suits the clay soils of the Marne Valley.

subregions.fact: Four main sub-regions: Montagne de Reims, Marne Valley (Vallée de la Marne), Côte des Blancs, Côte des Bar. The vineyard spans 319 villages ('crus') in five départements (Marne, Aube, Aisne, Haute-Marne, Seine-et-Marne).

classification.fact: Grand Cru: a former designation that 17 crus in Champagne have kept to this day.
Premier Cru: a former designation that 42 crus in Champagne have kept to this day.

The old 'échelle des crus' rated each village 80-100%. A 1952 decree reserved 'grand cru' for 100%-rated villages and 'premier cru' for 90-100%. INAO scrapped the scale in 2010 but let those villages keep the terms.
A 'cru' in Champagne is a winegrowing municipality; there are 319.

method.fact: Méthode Champenoise: first fermentation in tank turns must into still wine; second fermentation in bottle ('prise de mousse') makes it sparkling.
Liqueur de tirage: yeasts, sugar and wine added to the cuvée to trigger the second fermentation in bottle.
Remuage (riddling): rotating bottles after lees maturation so the deposit collects in the neck; automated riddling is now the norm.
Dosage: right after disgorgement the bottle is topped up with liqueur d'expédition, a mix of cane sugar and wine; the amount sets the style.
Minimum ageing: non-vintage at least 15 months and vintage at least 3 years, from the date of bottling.
method.note: CMS states NV 12 months on lees / 15 months total, vintage 36 months total.

method.fact: Grapes must be hand-picked: the rules require whole clusters to reach the press.

label_terms_styles.fact: Dosage levels (sugar per litre): Brut Nature / Pas Dosé / Dosage Zéro under 3 g/L with no added sugar; Extra-Brut 0-6 g/L; Brut under 12 g/L; Extra-Dry 12-17 g/L; Sec 17-32 g/L; Demi-Sec 32-50 g/L; Doux over 50 g/L (sweetest).
Non-vintage Brut is the most common Champagne: a blend of several years, the house's signature style. No year can be shown.
Vintage Champagne is made only from wines of one harvest year, shown on the bottle, with no reserve wines; made when the harvest is outstanding.
Blanc de Blancs: only white grapes (Chardonnay and/or, rarely, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Arbane or Petit Meslier). Blanc de Noirs: only black grapes (Pinot Noir and/or Meunier).
Rosé Champagne is made by maceration of black grapes or by blending red Champagne wine into the white base wines (about 5-20%).

Label producer codes: NM Négociant-Manipulant (buys grapes/wine; all big houses), RM Récoltant-Manipulant (grower using only own grapes), RC Récoltant-Coopérateur, CM Coopérative de Manipulation, SR Société de Récoltants, ND Négociant Distributeur, MA Marque d'Acheteur (buyer's own brand).
Bottles are built to withstand 20 bar, three times the natural pressure of Champagne.

must_know.fact: Brut means under 12 g/L sugar; Doux (over 50 g/L) is the sweetest; Brut Nature is under 3 g/L with no dosage.
17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru villages.
Main grapes: Pinot Noir, Meunier (black) and Chardonnay (white); most Champagne is white even though two of the three are black grapes.

location_climate.fact: Bourgogne is 230 km long, an hour from Lyon and two from Paris; 28,841 hectares under vine (3% of French commercial vineyards).
location_climate.note: The BIVB vineyards page gives 28,715 ha.

location_climate.fact: BIVB areas, north to south: Chablis & Grand Auxerrois; Châtillonnais; Côte de Nuits & Hautes Côtes de Nuits; Côte de Beaune & Hautes Côtes de Beaune; Côte Chalonnaise & Couchois; Mâconnais.
location_climate.note: Beaujolais is promoted separately by Inter Beaujolais. CMS's five regions are Chablis, Côte d'Or, Côte Chalonnaise, Mâconnais, Beaujolais.

location_climate.fact: Climate at the meeting point of continental, oceanic and southerly/Mediterranean influences; mainly temperate; about 700 mm rain a year; vines at 200-500 m on slopes.
Chablis, Grand Auxerrois and Châtillonnais: mainly semi-continental, more prone to spring frost. Mâconnais: hotter and drier, Mediterranean influence, harvest often about a week earlier.
CMS: five non-contiguous regions in eastern France; cool continental.

grapes.fact: Chardonnay (white) 57% of vineyard area; Pinot Noir (red) 34%; Aligoté (white) 6%; others (Gamay, Sauvignon, César, Pinot Beurot, Sacy, Melon, etc.) 3%.
Production by colour: white 62%, Crémant de Bourgogne 8%, red 29%, rosé 1%. Wines are mainly single-varietal.
Gamay: Philippe the Bold banned it from the Duchy of Burgundy in 1395; it moved to the south of the region and Beaujolais. It is now the red grape of the Mâconnais.
Bouzeron (Côte Chalonnaise) is the only Village appellation made exclusively from Aligoté (AOC 1997).

appellations_subregions.fact: Côte de Nuits (Dijon to Corgoloin, about 20 km): the centre of the region's Grands Crus, mainly red from Pinot Noir. Village appellations include Chambolle-Musigny, Fixin, Gevrey-Chambertin, Marsannay, Morey-Saint-Denis, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Vosne-Romanée, Vougeot.

Côte de Beaune (Ladoix-Serrigny to Maranges, about 20 km): around Beaune mainly Pinot Noir (Volnay, Pommard); from Meursault south, Chardonnay dominates. Grands Crus: Corton, Corton-Charlemagne, Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet.
Montrachet is the cradle of five white Grands Crus: Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet.
Côte Chalonnaise Village appellations: Bouzeron, Givry, Mercurey, Montagny, Rully. Thought to be the cradle of Crémant de Bourgogne (AOC 1975).
Mâconnais: Chardonnay is 80% of vines; reds mainly Gamay. Village appellations: Pouilly-Fuissé, Pouilly-Loché, Pouilly-Vinzelles, Saint-Véran, Viré-Clessé.

classification.fact: Burgundy has exactly 84 AOCs, more than 23% of all French wine AOCs. Four levels: Régionale, Village, Village Premier Cru, Grand Cru.

7 Régionale appellations (e.g. Bourgogne Aligoté, Mâcon Village, Coteaux Bourguignons, Crémant de Bourgogne); 44 Village appellations named after their commune (e.g. Mercurey, Pommard, Nuits-Saint-Georges); 33 Grand Cru appellations.
Premier Cru wines come from single precisely defined plots (Climats) within a Village appellation; the label shows the commune then the Climat, e.g. 'Chablis Premier Cru, Montée de Tonnerre'.
Grand Cru labels replace the village name with the single Climat name, e.g. Corton, Montrachet, Romanée Saint-Vivant, Clos de Tart.

CMS hierarchy: Regional AOP / Villages AOP / Premier Cru AOP / Grand Cru AOP; Côte d'Or consists of two regional AOPs, Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune, each with Village / Premier Cru / Grand Cru AOPs.

chablis.fact: Chablis: one colour (white), one grape (Chardonnay), four levels of appellation.
The four Chablis appellations: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru, Chablis Grand Cru.
Chablis Grand Cru has seven Climats: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir. AOC created 1938; about 1% of Chablis; 99 ha (2025).
Chablis Premier Cru: 40 Climats including 17 main 'flag-bearing' ones; AOC 1967; about 13% of Chablis.

Soils: Kimmeridgian limestone and marl with small Exogyra virgula oyster fossils (Chablis, Premier Cru, Grand Cru on the hillsides); harder Portlandian limestone mainly for Petit Chablis on higher slopes and plateau.
Climate described as semi-continental (or 'modified oceanic'); spring frost is the classic hazard, fought with heaters, candles, heated cables and water spraying.

beaujolais.fact: Beaujolais runs from south of Mâcon to north of Lyon: 13,500 ha in 12 AOCs, almost all Gamay (97%).

The 12 AOCs: Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages, and the 10 crus Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Côte de Brouilly, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié, Saint-Amour. Regional AOCs lie mainly in the south (clay, some limestone); the crus are in the north (often sandy soils of granitic origin).
Morgon is the largest Beaujolais cru; its famous Côte du Py is decomposed shale. Morgon soils: granite 52%, blue stone 37%, piedmont deposits 11%.
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November.

label_terms_styles.fact: CMS Intro label terms: Négociant, Domaine, Clos, Monopole, Vieilles Vignes.
'Climats' in Burgundy are plots of vines delimited by winemakers over generations; there are more than a thousand.
The Climats of Bourgogne are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

must_know.fact: Red Burgundy is Pinot Noir; white Burgundy is Chardonnay (Chablis is 100% Chardonnay).
Burgundy hierarchy: Régionale > Village > Premier Cru > Grand Cru (33 Grands Crus, 84 AOCs in total).
Chablis Grand Cru = 7 Climats on Kimmeridgian soil; Beaujolais = Gamay, 10 crus.

location_climate.fact: CMS: Southwest France along the Atlantic coast; climate maritime to continental moving inland. Key waters: Atlantic Ocean, Gironde Estuary, Garonne River, Dordogne River.

The Médoc sits on the Left Bank between the ocean and the Gironde estuary; Graves-Sauternes is on the Left Bank between the Garonne and the Ciron; Entre-Deux-Mers lies between the Dordogne and the Garonne.
location_climate.note: Graves and Entre-Deux-Mers positions from the bordeaux.com Graves-Sauternes and Entre-Deux-Mers pages.

location_climate.fact: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac (the Right Bank) are a patchwork of limestone plateaus, molasse and clay soils, shaped by Merlot and lifted by the Cabernets.
Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac lie along the Dordogne.

grapes.fact: Six main grapes, three red and three white. Red plantings: Merlot 66%, Cabernet Sauvignon 22.5%, Cabernet Franc 9.5%; auxiliary reds (Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carménère) 2%.
White plantings: Sauvignon Blanc 45%, Sémillon 42%, Muscadelle 5%; auxiliary whites (Colombard, Merlot Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Ugni Blanc) 8%.
Bordeaux wines are most often blends of several varieties.
CMS: Cabernet Sauvignon is matched to gravel, Merlot to clay.

subregions_appellations.fact: Six winegrowing areas on bordeaux.com: Bordeaux/Bordeaux Supérieur/Crémant; Graves-Sauternes; Entre-Deux-Mers/Premières Côtes/Sainte-Foy; Saint-Émilion/Pomerol/Fronsac; Médoc; Blaye-Bourg.
Médoc appellations: Médoc, Haut-Médoc, Listrac-Médoc, Moulis, Margaux, Pauillac, Saint-Estèphe, Saint-Julien. The Médoc makes only red wines.
Graves-Sauternes appellations include Graves, Graves Supérieures, Pessac-Léognan, Sauternes, Barsac and Cérons: reds, dry whites and sweet wines.
Entre-Deux-Mers is known for dry whites; Cadillac, Loupiac, Sainte-Croix-du-Mont and neighbours make sweet wines shaped by noble rot.
Pomerol: red only; 813 ha; Merlot about 80%, Cabernet Franc 15%, Cabernet Sauvignon 5%; one of Bordeaux's smallest appellations (0.7%).

classification.fact: Five Bordeaux classifications: 1855; Graves; Saint-Émilion; Crus Bourgeois du Médoc; Crus Artisans.
1855: Napoleon III asked for a ranking for the Paris Universal Exhibition; Bordeaux brokers ranked by reputation and market price. Published 18 April 1855.

1855 has 88 classified growths: reds in five levels (Premier to Cinquième Cru) - 60 Médoc estates plus Château Haut-Brion in Graves (Pessac); sweet whites in three levels (Premier Cru Supérieur, Premier Cru, Second Cru) - 27 châteaux in Sauternes and Barsac.
The five First Growths (Premiers Crus): Château Lafite-Rothschild (Pauillac), Château Latour (Pauillac), Château Margaux (Margaux), Château Mouton Rothschild (Pauillac), Château Haut-Brion (Pessac).
Only two changes to the 1855 list in 150 years: Mouton Rothschild's promotion in June 1973, and Cantemerle's addition to the Fifth Growths on 16 September 1855. (Translated from French.)
Sauternes and Barsac 1855: the single Premier Cru Supérieur is Château d'Yquem (Sauternes).
Graves classification: 14 châteaux, all in Pessac-Léognan, classified for red, white or both; first list 1953, one change 1959; Haut-Brion is in both Graves and 1855 lists.

Saint-Émilion classification: first in 1955, revised every ten years. Three levels: Premiers Grands Crus Classés 'A', Premiers Grands Crus Classés, Grands Crus Classés. 2022 (7th edition): 85 properties - 2 'A', 12 Premiers Grands Crus Classés, 71 Grands Crus Classés.
2022 Premiers Grands Crus Classés 'A': Château Figeac and Château Pavie.
Château Ausone, Château Cheval Blanc and Château Angélus do not appear on the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification list.
classification.note: Absence checked on the list; the reason is not stated on the pages fetched.

classification.fact: Saint-Émilion has two AOCs, Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru; the Grand Cru AOC allows the titles 'Grand Cru Classé' and 'Premier Grand Cru Classé'.
Crus Bourgeois du Médoc: three levels (Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur, Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel); revised every five years since 2020; 170 estates in 2025.
Pomerol: no classification.

label_terms_styles.fact: CMS styles: appellation-dependent, from dry reds and dry whites to lusciously sweet whites; botrytis-affected sweet wines (Sauternes); new French oak used for reds and whites.
'Grand Cru Classé en 1855' appears on labels of 1855-classified châteaux.

must_know.fact: Five First Growths: Lafite-Rothschild, Latour, Margaux, Mouton Rothschild (promoted 1973), Haut-Brion (the only one outside the Médoc).
Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape (66% of red plantings); Left Bank leans Cabernet Sauvignon on gravel, Right Bank Merlot on clay/limestone.
Château d'Yquem is the only Premier Cru Supérieur (Sauternes); Saint-Émilion's list is revised every ten years, Pomerol has none.

location_climate.fact: CMS: from the Atlantic coast to central France; the Loire is France's longest river, rising in the Massif Central. Regions west to east: Pays Nantais, Anjou-Saumur, Touraine, Central Vineyards.
Loire vineyards cover about 42,000 ha in 14 départements, the 3rd largest wine region in France; 34 AOPs plus the Val de Loire IGP; white is the dominant colour.
Climate: oceanic around Nantes and Anjou (mild winters, temperate summers); semi-oceanic in Saumur and western Touraine; more continental in Touraine and Haut-Poitou.
Soils: granite, gneiss and schist of the Armorican Massif (Nantes, western Anjou); schist and tuffeau in Anjou-Saumur; sands and flinty clays in Touraine.

grapes.fact: More than 100 grape varieties, 7 major: Cabernet Franc, Chenin Blanc, Melon Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Gamay Noir, Chardonnay, Grolleau Noir.

Chenin (Pineau de la Loire) is native to the Loire: early-picked for dry and sparkling, late-picked for sweet. Melon B is the only grape of Muscadet. Cabernet Franc is the Loire's leading red (Saumur-Champigny, Chinon, Bourgueil, St-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil, Anjou).
Centre-Loire specialises in white from Sauvignon Blanc and red/rosé from Pinot Noir.

subregions_appellations.fact: Muscadet is a dry white from Melon de Bourgogne, often matured 'sur lie'. Nantes appellations include Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine, Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire, Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu, Gros Plant du Pays Nantais (Folle Blanche) and Coteaux d'Ancenis.
Muscadet AOC has been an official appellation since 1937 (1,300 ha); its subsoil is based on the Armorican Massif (gneiss, micaschist, gabbro). Grape: Melon B.
Anjou-Saumur famous appellations: Saumur, Anjou, Savennières, Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume; Bonnezeaux and Coteaux du Layon are Chenin.
Touraine runs from Montsoreau to Blois along the Loire and has 17 appellations, including Chinon, Vouvray and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil.
Touraine: Vouvray is famous for whites; Chinon and Bourgueil for reds. Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas de Bourgueil are listed as Cabernet Franc; Chinon as Chenin and Cabernet Franc.
Vouvray: grape variety Chenin; colours white and fine bubbles (sparkling); styles listed: dry, sweet/liquoreux and sparkling; 7 communes on the right bank of the Loire.

Sancerre: about 3,000 ha on the left bank of the Loire; white from Sauvignon Blanc (AOC 1936), red and rosé from Pinot Noir (AOC 1959). Soils: terres blanches (clay-limestone), caillottes (pebbly), and siliceous-clay soils.
Pouilly-Fumé is 100% Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-sur-Loire is Chasselas only; both AOC 1937, on the right bank of the Loire.
Quincy was the first Centre-Loire AOC (August 1936); Menetou-Salon and Reuilly are other Centre-Loire Sauvignon Blanc appellations.

classification.fact: Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru: sweet Chenin from a small part of Rochefort-sur-Loire on the right bank of the Layon; described as one of France's most prestigious sweet AOPs.
Coteaux du Layon has a '1er Cru Chaume' appellation; Savennières has 'Roche aux Moines'; Coulée de Serrant is a 7-hectare biodynamic appellation.

label_terms_styles.fact: Sweet terms: moelleux = moderate residual sugar 10-45 g/L; liquoreux = over 45 g/L. (Translated from the French page.)

Loire sweet whites come from botrytis (noble rot) or passerillage on late-picked Chenin; appellations include Bonnezeaux, Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, Coteaux de l'Aubance, Vouvray moelleux.
Loire sparkling wines use the traditional method; minimum 9 months on laths for Crémant de Loire and 12 months for Vouvray.
CMS label terms: Sur lie, Sec, Demi-Sec (Intro); Moelleux (Certified).

must_know.fact: Muscadet = Melon B, often 'sur lie'; Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé = Sauvignon Blanc; Vouvray = Chenin; Chinon and Bourgueil = Cabernet Franc.
Botrytis sweet Chenin: Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux, Coteaux du Layon.
Pouilly-Fumé (Sauvignon Blanc) is not Pouilly-Fuissé (Burgundy, Chardonnay).
must_know.note: Pouilly-Fuissé as a Mâconnais village appellation is on the BIVB Mâconnais page.

location_climate.fact: Alsace lies between the Rhine river and the Vosges mountains, on the borders of Germany and Switzerland.
Sheltered from oceanic influences by the Vosges, Alsace has one of France's lowest rainfalls and a semi-continental climate that is sunny, warm and dry. Vineyards sit on hills at 200-400 m.
location_climate.note: The same page gives rainfall as 500-600 mm in one place and 600-650 mm in another.

location_climate.fact: West winds drop their rain on the western slopes of the Vosges and arrive dry over the vineyards (rain shadow).
CMS: over 90% of Alsace wine is from white grapes; best vineyards face east/southeast.

grapes.fact: Seven major grape varieties, which give Alsace wines their names.
Wines listed by Vins d'Alsace: Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Sylvaner, Muscat, Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer (whites); Pinot Noir (rosé and red); blends Edelzwicker and Gentil; Crémant d'Alsace.
CMS: varietal-labelled wines must be 100% of the named grape. Intro grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat (white); Pinot Noir (red).

appellations.fact: AOC Alsace (recognised 1962): over 70% of production. Since 2011 it can add a commune or lieu-dit name.
AOC Crémant d'Alsace (1976): about a quarter of production.
51 Alsace Grands Crus, each its own appellation since 2011; about 5% of production. Sites classified 1975-2007, 3 to 80 ha each.

classification.fact: Grand Cru grapes: Riesling, Muscat, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer; exception: Sylvaner allowed in Zotzenberg; co-planting practised in Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf.
CMS adds Pinot Noir as a fifth Grand Cru grape from the 2022 vintage, with two Grands Crus allowing red wine.
classification.note: Not stated on the vinsalsace.com pages fetched.

label_terms_styles.fact: Vendanges Tardives (since 1984): great sweet wines from over-ripe grapes; may be added to Alsace or Alsace Grand Cru labels.
Sélection de Grains Nobles (since 1984): sumptuous sweet wines from carefully hand-picked berries; for SGN only noble-rot (botrytis) berries are kept.
label_terms_styles.note: Botrytis detail from the Grands Crus page.

label_terms_styles.fact: VT and SGN are harvested over-ripe in very good years.
Edelzwicker and Gentil are Alsace blends.
CMS: Alsace AOP wines must be bottled in the traditional 'Vin du Rhin' / 'Flûte d'Alsace' bottle (Certified column).

must_know.fact: 51 Grands Crus; four classic Grand Cru grapes Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat.
VT = late harvest; SGN = noble-rot selected berries; both since 1984.
Vosges rain shadow makes Alsace one of France's driest regions.

location_climate.fact: The Rhône Valley vineyards run between Vienne and Avignon across six départements (Ardèche, Drôme, Gard, Loire, Rhône, Vaucluse), bordered by the Massif Central, the Alps and the Mediterranean.
Described by Inter Rhône as France's second AOC vineyard.
CMS: Northern Rhône moderate continental, steep hillsides; Southern Rhône Mediterranean, flatter; a 30-mile gap between them.
Mistral: dry north wind characteristic of the Southern Rhône's Mediterranean climate, sometimes over 100 km/h; dries vines after rain.
Soils: north - granite, schist, limestone; south - sand, marl, white limestone, clays, rounded pebbles, gravel.

grapes.fact: North: Syrah for reds; Viognier and Marsanne dominate whites. South: Grenache Noir blended with Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Cinsault for reds and rosés; whites from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Marsanne, Roussanne, Viognier.
Cornas reds are single-varietal (Syrah); Côte-Rôtie, Saint-Joseph, Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage allow single-varietal or blends; Condrieu and Château-Grillet whites are Viognier.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape lists 18 associated varieties: Bourboulenc, Brun Argenté (Camarèse/Vaccarèse), Cinsault, Clairette Blanche, Clairette Rose, Counoise, Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Grenache Noir, Mourvèdre, Muscardin, Picardan, Piquepoul Blanc, Piquepoul Gris, Piquepoul Noir, Roussanne, Syrah, Terret Noir. Grenache Noir dominates.

appellations_classification.fact: Appellation tiers on Inter Rhône: Côtes du Rhône AOC; Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC (some with a named village, e.g. Côtes du Rhône Villages Chusclan, Gadagne, Massif d'Uchaux); Côtes du Rhône Crus; plus other Rhône Valley AOCs and Vins Doux Naturels.
A cru is a communal AOC at the top of the hierarchy; 1 cru = 1 AOC. Northern crus: Château-Grillet, Condrieu, Cornas, Côte-Rôtie, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Saint-Joseph, Saint-Péray.

Southern crus named in the Inter Rhône glossary: Beaumes-de-Venise, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Laudun, Lirac, Rasteau, Tavel, Vacqueyras, Vinsobres. Inter Rhône's grape filter also lists 'Côtes du Rhône Cru AOC Cairanne'.
appellations_classification.note: Cairanne is missing from the glossary list but present on the grape-varieties page filter.

appellations_classification.fact: Châteauneuf-du-Pape: cru since 1936 (decree of 15 May 1936), red and white still wines, 5 communes in Vaucluse on the left bank; Mediterranean climate with Mistral, under 650 mm rain and about 2,800 sunshine hours; soils of rolled pebbles with red clay, sand and sandstone.
appellations_classification.note: The Inter Rhône history page says CdP secured AOC status in 1933.

appellations_classification.fact: Vins Doux Naturels: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau, made by mutage (adding alcohol to stop fermentation).

label_terms_styles.fact: CMS Intro: Vins Doux Naturels (example Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise); Cru = single village; style: spicy, meaty reds; rich, aromatic whites.
History: 14th-century Avignon papacy; Pope John XXII built a summer residence at Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

must_know.fact: North = Syrah (reds) and Viognier (Condrieu); South = Grenache-based blends (Châteauneuf-du-Pape).
The Mistral is the cold, dry north wind of the Southern Rhône.
Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is a Vin Doux Naturel made by mutage.

conflicts_between_sources.fact: Champagne plantings: 38/32/30 (Pinot Noir/Chardonnay/Meunier, 2025 at-a-glance) vs 38/31/31 (grape page) vs CMS 38/30 Chardonnay/32 Meunier.
Champagne area: 34,200 ha (FAQ, at-a-glance) vs 34,300 ha (region page); crus 319 vs 'Total crus: 320' in a figure box on the region page.
Champagne minor grapes: FAQ lists four (Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris); grape page adds Chardonnay Rose (authorised 2025).
Champagne ageing: champagne.fr gives NV 15 months and vintage 3 years from bottling; CMS gives NV 12 months on lees / 15 total and vintage 36 months total.

1855 changes: CMS says only one change (Mouton 1973); the Conseil des Grands Crus Classés en 1855 says two (Mouton 1973 and Cantemerle added 16 Sept 1855). bordeaux.com says the 1855 classification 'never changes'.
Burgundy area: 28,841 ha (locating page) vs 28,715 ha (vineyards page).
Rhône crus: Inter Rhône glossary lists 17 crus (8 north, 9 south) without Cairanne; its appellation/grape filter includes 'Côtes du Rhône Cru AOC Cairanne' (18).
Châteauneuf-du-Pape AOC date: 15 May 1936 decree (CdP page) vs 1933 (Inter Rhône history page).
Alsace rainfall: 500-600 mm and 600-650 mm both appear on the same Vins d'Alsace page.

unverified.fact: Number of Burgundy Premier Cru Climats. Search snippets gave conflicting figures (562, about 640, 666); no BIVB page fetched states a number.

Pinot Noir as an Alsace Grand Cru grape from the 2022 vintage: stated by the CMS Curriculum Guide, not found on the vinsalsace.com pages fetched. Trade-press search results name Kirchberg de Barr and Hengst, but those pages were not fetched.
Madame Clicquot inventing the riddling rack: stated by the CMS Curriculum Guide only; the champagne.fr history page fetched does not mention it.
Sugar thresholds for Loire 'sec' and 'demi-sec': not stated on the InterLoire pages fetched (only moelleux 10-45 g/L and liquoreux over 45 g/L).
Why Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus are absent from the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification: not stated on the pages fetched.
Bordeaux climate from a Bordeaux body (CIVB): the bordeaux.com pages fetched do not describe the climate; the manual uses the CMS description.
Total number of Bordeaux appellations: not found on bordeaux.com pages fetched.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape minimum alcohol and Southern Rhône minimum Grenache rules: listed as Certified-level topics by CMS; not verified.

Burgundy 'five regions': CMS counts Chablis, Côte d'Or, Côte Chalonnaise, Mâconnais, Beaujolais; BIVB lists six areas without Beaujolais (and its pages also say 'five wine-producing regions'). Treat the CMS grouping as the exam view.
